lessonTitle: Gastrointestinal, Hepatic and Renal Pathology: Cirrhosis, Glomerular Syndromes and the Adenoma-Carcinoma Sequence

blocks.text: A 12-year-old boy wakes with puffy eyelids and frothy urine, while an adult with dark, smoky urine and high blood pressure is seen the same week. Both have kidney disease, but the glomeruli are injured in opposite ways. Reading a biopsy of the liver, kidney or colon means asking the same question: what pattern of damage is this, and what mechanism produced it?

blocks.markdown: This unit covers three organ systems where tissue pattern explains the clinical picture: scarring of the liver (cirrhosis and chronic hepatitis), glomerular disease (nephritic versus nephrotic), and the stepwise genetic and histological progression from colorectal adenoma to carcinoma.

blocks.title: Cirrhosis
blocks.text: Cirrhosis is a diffuse process in which fibrosis (bridging fibrous septa) divides the liver into regenerative nodules of hepatocytes and destroys the normal lobular architecture. Three features are all required: it is diffuse (not a single scar), there is fibrosis, and there are regenerative nodules. It is the end stage of many chronic injuries such as alcohol, chronic viral hepatitis and fatty liver disease.

blocks.markdown: **Chronic hepatitis** is hepatic inflammation lasting more than 6 months. Histology shows a lymphocytic infiltrate in the portal tracts, **interface hepatitis** (inflammatory cells crossing the limiting plate with death of adjacent hepatocytes, formerly called piecemeal necrosis), and in worse disease **bridging necrosis** linking portal tracts and central veins. Pathologists report **grade** (necroinflammatory activity, which is potentially reversible) separately from **stage** (extent of fibrosis from none to cirrhosis, which determines prognosis). Hepatitis B may show **ground-glass hepatocytes** from surface antigen accumulation; hepatitis C often shows portal lymphoid aggregates and steatosis.

rows: Portal lymphocytes, interface hepatitis, variable fibrosis
Hepatitis B or C, autoimmune hepatitis
Nodules over 3 mm of variable size
Neutrophils, ballooned hepatocytes, Mallory-Denk bodies, steatosis
Heavy alcohol intake; serum AST:ALT ratio typically above 2

blocks.title: Reading a chronic hepatitis biopsy
blocks.prompt: A liver biopsy from a 47-year-old shows dense portal lymphocytes, interface hepatitis, fibrous septa linking portal tracts but no regenerative nodules, and hepatocytes with homogeneous pale cytoplasm. State the grade of activity and stage of disease in words and name the likely cause.

steps.text: Dense portal inflammation with interface hepatitis indicates high necroinflammatory activity (high grade).
Septa that bridge portal tracts show advanced fibrosis, but no nodules means the criteria for cirrhosis are not met.
Bridging fibrosis without cirrhosis corresponds to a stage just below cirrhosis (stage 3 of 4 on a 0 to 4 scale).
Homogeneous pale (ground-glass) cytoplasm suggests accumulated hepatitis B surface antigen.

blocks.answer: Active chronic hepatitis (high grade) with bridging fibrosis (stage 3 of 4), not yet cirrhosis, probably due to hepatitis B.

blocks.markdown: **Glomerular disease.** The glomerular filtration barrier has three layers: fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and podocyte foot processes. Inflammation of the glomerulus causes the **nephritic syndrome**; damage to the barrier without much inflammation causes the **nephrotic syndrome**. Nephrotic syndrome in adults is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g per 24 hours, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Nephritic syndrome presents with haematuria (red cell casts), hypertension, reduced urine output and raised creatinine, with proteinuria usually below the nephrotic range.

blocks.caption: Nephrotic range in adults is above 3.5 g/day.

rows: Loss of barrier selectivity, little inflammation
Haematuria, red cell casts, modest proteinuria
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: subepithelial humps, hypercellular glomeruli
Minimal change disease: normal light microscopy, foot process effacement on electron microscopy
Membranous nephropathy: thick GBM, subepithelial deposits (spike and dome)
blocks.caption: Nephritic versus nephrotic glomerular disease.

blocks.title: Is this proteinuria nephrotic range?
blocks.prompt: A woman has swollen ankles. A 24-hour urine collection is 1.8 L and contains 2.4 g/L of protein. Her serum albumin is 24 g/L. Decide whether she meets the biochemical criteria for nephrotic syndrome.

steps.text: Use the equation for daily loss.
Compare with the threshold of 3.5 g/day: 4.32 is higher.
Serum albumin of 24 g/L is low (reference range varies by laboratory, around 35 to 50 g/L), and oedema is present.

blocks.answer: Daily protein loss is 4.32 g, which exceeds 3.5 g/day; with hypoalbuminaemia and oedema this is nephrotic syndrome.

blocks.markdown: **The adenoma-carcinoma sequence.** Most colorectal cancers arise from a benign adenoma (dysplastic glandular epithelium) over roughly a decade or more, accumulating mutations. Loss of function of the **APC** tumour suppressor gene is the usual first step: APC normally degrades beta-catenin, so loss lets beta-catenin drive proliferation, forming small adenomas. Activating **KRAS** mutation then promotes growth of larger adenomas, loss of SMAD4 and chromosome 18q follows, and inactivation of **TP53** is typically late and marks progression to invasive carcinoma. Larger size (over 1 cm), villous architecture and high-grade dysplasia increase cancer risk.

rows: Invasive adenocarcinoma through the muscularis mucosae
blocks.caption: A simplified model: the order varies and several pathways exist.

blocks.title: Mechanism links to appearance
blocks.text: Nodules plus bridging fibrosis define cirrhosis, inflammation separates nephritic from nephrotic disease, and accumulating mutations explain why adenomas are removed. Invasion through the muscularis mucosae, not dysplasia alone, defines carcinoma.

points: Cirrhosis is diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules; chronic hepatitis is graded for activity and staged for fibrosis.
Nephritic disease is inflammatory with haematuria and hypertension; nephrotic disease has proteinuria above 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
The adenoma-carcinoma sequence accumulates APC loss, KRAS activation and TP53 loss over years, so detecting and removing adenomas prevents cancer.

questions.stem: Which combination is required to call a liver biopsy cirrhosis?

options.text: Diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules and architectural distortion
Fat droplets in more than 5% of hepatocytes

questions.correctOptionText: Diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules and architectural distortion

distractorRationale.a: Correct: all three features and a diffuse distribution.
distractorRationale.b: A focal scar is not diffuse cirrhosis.
distractorRationale.c: This is chronic inflammation, which can occur without cirrhosis.
distractorRationale.d: This is steatosis, which can occur without cirrhosis.

questions.explanation: Cirrhosis is a diffuse process combining fibrosis and nodular regeneration that disrupts the lobular architecture. Inflammation or fat without nodules and septa does not qualify.

questions.stem: A hepatitis C biopsy report states 'grade 3 of 4, stage 1 of 4'. What does this indicate?

options.text: Marked inflammatory activity with only mild fibrosis

questions.correctOptionText: Marked inflammatory activity with only mild fibrosis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: grade is activity and stage is fibrosis.

questions.explanation: Grade describes necroinflammatory activity and stage describes fibrosis. High grade with low stage means active inflammation with little scarring so far, which is potentially reversible with treatment.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old develops tea-coloured urine, hypertension and oliguria 2 weeks after a sore throat. Which biopsy finding is expected?

options.text: Normal light microscopy with foot process effacement
Spike and dome pattern in a thick GBM

distractorRationale.b: This is minimal change disease, which is nephrotic.
distractorRationale.c: This is membranous nephropathy, which is nephrotic.
distractorRationale.d: Amyloid is not suggested by this picture.

questions.explanation: The haematuria, hypertension and oliguria after a streptococcal infection indicate nephritic syndrome. Immune complexes deposit subepithelially as humps and the glomeruli are hypercellular.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has generalised oedema and heavy proteinuria. Light microscopy is normal and electron microscopy shows diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes. Which is the diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: normal light microscopy with foot process effacement.
distractorRationale.b: This is nephritic with a hypercellular glomerulus.
distractorRationale.c: This shows mesangial IgA deposits and haematuria.
distractorRationale.d: This shows thick GBM with deposits, typically in adults.

questions.explanation: Minimal change disease is the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. The glomerulus looks normal by light microscopy and the lesion is only seen on electron microscopy.

questions.stem: Which molecular event is classically the earliest step in the adenoma-carcinoma sequence?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: APC loss activates beta-catenin signalling and starts adenoma formation.
distractorRationale.c: HER2 amplification is not the classic initiating event here.
distractorRationale.d: RB loss is not the classic colorectal initiating event.

questions.explanation: APC loss initiates dysplasia by allowing beta-catenin accumulation. TP53 loss comes later and is associated with progression to invasive carcinoma.

questions.stem: In the adenoma-carcinoma sequence, TP53 inactivation typically occurs late and is associated with progression to invasive carcinoma.
questions.explanation: Early steps such as APC loss produce adenomas, while TP53 loss removes the cell-cycle checkpoint and apoptosis response, allowing invasive cancer. The sequence is thus a gradual accumulation of mutations.

questions.stem: A patient with leg swelling has a 24-hour urine volume of 1.5 L with a protein concentration of 1.6 g/L. Calculate the daily protein loss in g/day. (Nephrotic range in adults is above 3.5 g/day.)
questions.explanation: Daily loss is 1.6 g/L times 1.5 L, which is 2.4 g/day. This is below 3.5 g/day, so it is not in the nephrotic range.

questions.stem: In alcoholic liver disease the serum AST:ALT ratio is typically above 2. A patient has AST 168 U/L and ALT 64 U/L. Calculate the AST:ALT ratio (dimensionless).
questions.explanation: The ratio is 168 divided by 64, which is 2.625. A ratio above 2 supports alcohol-related injury with ballooned hepatocytes and neutrophils on histology, rather than viral hepatitis.

questions.stem: Two patients are admitted. Patient A (27) has haematuria, blood pressure 170/100 mmHg and 0.5 g/day proteinuria. Patient B (62) has 6 g/day proteinuria, albumin 20 g/L and ankle oedema. Explain the pathological and clinical differences between nephritic and nephrotic disease with reference to these patients.
markingGuide: A is nephritic: glomerular inflammation and hypercellularity
B is nephrotic: loss of barrier selectivity with little inflammation
Haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, oliguria in nephritic disease
Proteinuria above 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia in nephrotic disease
Give an example of each, such as post-streptococcal GN and membranous nephropathy
Deposit pattern or EM finding for each example
questions.explanation: Inflammation leads to haematuria and hypertension, while loss of the barrier leads to protein loss and oedema. Marking should reward the mechanism linking each lesion to its clinical picture.

questions.stem: A 2.4 cm villous adenoma with high-grade dysplasia is removed at colonoscopy from a 61-year-old man. Explain the pathological basis of the adenoma-carcinoma sequence and why this polyp warrants removal and follow-up.
markingGuide: APC loss and beta-catenin activation initiate adenoma
KRAS activation and later events such as 18q loss increase growth and dysplasia
TP53 loss is late and permits invasion
Sequence takes years, which provides a window for screening
Size over 1 cm, villous architecture and high-grade dysplasia raise cancer risk
Carcinoma is defined by invasion through the muscularis mucosae
questions.explanation: The sequence is progressive accumulation of genetic damage, so large villous high-grade lesions are further along. Removing the adenoma interrupts the process before invasion.
